questions.topic: Intermolecular Forces in Sulfur and Oxygen
questions.question: Explain why sulfur is a solid and oxygen is a gas at room temperature and pressure, by referring to the intermolecular forces involved.
questions.answer: Sulfur (S8) has larger molecules with more electrons, so stronger London forces between molecules; O2 molecules are small with weak London forces, so it is a gas
steps: Sulfur exists as S8 molecules, which are large with many electrons
Larger molecules have larger, more polarisable electron clouds and stronger London (instantaneous induced dipole) forces
Stronger London forces need more energy to overcome, so sulfur is a solid at room temperature
Oxygen is a small O2 molecule with weak London forces only, so it is a gas

questions.topic: Temperature and Pressure in Contact Process
questions.question: Step 2 of the contact process is 2SO2 + O2 <=> 2SO3, a reversible reaction. State the effect on the position of equilibrium of increasing temperature at constant pressure, and of increasing pressure at constant temperature, and justify each answer.
questions.answer: Higher temperature shifts equilibrium to the left (forward reaction is exothermic); higher pressure shifts it to the right (3 mol gas to 2 mol gas)
steps: Step 2 forward reaction is exothermic (delta H negative)
Increasing temperature at constant pressure favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so the position moves left
Gas moles: 2 SO2 + 1 O2 = 3 mol on the left; 2 SO3 = 2 mol on the right
Increasing pressure at constant temperature favours the side with fewer gas moles, so the position moves right

questions.question: Explain how the use of a catalyst makes this reaction more sustainable.
questions.answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a lower temperature can be used, saving energy and reducing emissions; the catalyst is reused
steps: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reaction
The same rate can be reached at a lower temperature
Less energy (fuel) is needed, so fewer CO2 emissions are produced
The catalyst is not used up and can be reused, reducing waste

questions.question: Compare and contrast the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with solid potassium chloride and with solid potassium iodide, to show the difference in reducing ability of the halide ions. Describe what would be observed and identify the products.
questions.answer: KCl gives misty fumes of HCl (no redox); KI is oxidised to purple iodine vapour and I2, while H2SO4 is reduced to SO2, H2S and yellow sulfur; I- is the stronger reducing agent
steps: With KCl: acid-base reaction only, giving misty white fumes of HCl; Cl- is not oxidised (weak reducing agent)
With KI: I- is a stronger reducing agent and is oxidised to I2 (purple/violet vapour, black solid)
The sulfuric acid is reduced, forming SO2 (choking gas) and H2S (rotten egg smell)
Sulfur is also formed as a yellow solid, as H2SO4 is reduced further
Overall, iodide ions reduce concentrated sulfuric acid, but chloride ions do not, so I- is the stronger reducing agent
Reducing ability increases down Group 7 (Cl- < Br- < I-)

questions.question: A technician makes 500 cm3 of 1.5 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid by diluting 40.5 cm3 of concentrated sulfuric acid. Calculate the concentration of the concentrated acid in mol dm-3.
questions.answer: 18.5 mol dm-3
steps: Moles of H2SO4 in diluted solution = 1.5 x 0.500 = 0.75 mol
The same moles come from the concentrated acid (dilution does not change moles)
Concentration = moles / volume = 0.75 / 0.0405 dm3
Concentration = 18.5 mol dm-3

questions.question: A student burns 0.305 g of ethanol to heat 100.0 g of water, which rises by 13.2 C (specific heat capacity 4.18 J g-1 C-1). Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol with sign and units, to an appropriate number of significant figures.
questions.answer: -832 kJ mol-1
steps: Heat absorbed by water q = m c delta T = 100.0 x 4.18 x 13.2 = 5518 J (5.52 kJ)
Mr of ethanol C2H5OH = 46.0; moles = 0.305 / 46.0 = 6.63 x 10^-3 mol
Enthalpy change per mole = 5.518 / 6.63 x 10^-3 = 832 kJ mol-1 released
Combustion releases heat, so delta cH = -832 kJ mol-1 (3 s.f.)

questions.question: The uncertainty in each thermometer reading is 0.05 C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise of 13.2 C.

questions.question: The data book value for the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is more exothermic than the experimental value. Give two reasons for the difference, other than standard conditions.

Some heat is absorbed by the copper or glass apparatus, not only the water
Ethanol burns incompletely (soot), so less heat is released per mole
Some ethanol evaporates before it burns, so the mass burned is less than the mass recorded

questions.topic: NO2 and N2O4 Equilibrium on Compression
questions.question: NO2 and N2O4 are in equilibrium in a gas syringe (pale brown). When the mixture is compressed, the colour becomes: A darker, B lighter, C darker and then lighter, D lighter and then darker.
questions.answer: C (darker and then lighter)

The equilibrium 2NO2 <=> N2O4 shifts right to reduce the gas moles (2 mol to 1 mol)
NO2 (brown) is used up, so the colour gets lighter again, though not as light as before

questions.answer: B (high temperature, low pressure)

The forward reaction makes 2 mol gas from 0 mol gas
Low pressure favours the side with more gas moles, so the forward reaction gives higher yield

questions.question: The same procedure is used for strontium hydroxide. Explain whether the mean titre would be different from that for calcium hydroxide.
questions.answer: Yes, the titre would be different: Sr(OH)2 is more soluble than Ca(OH)2, so its saturated solution has a higher concentration of OH- and a larger titre
steps: Both hydroxides react with HCl in the same 1:2 ratio, so the titre depends on the concentration of OH- in the saturated solution
Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group
Sr(OH)2 is more soluble than Ca(OH)2, so its saturated solution has more OH- per dm3
A larger volume of acid is needed, so the titre is larger

questions.question: Explain, in terms of the equilibrium of carbonic acid, the effect of the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide on the acidity of seawater. (CO2 dissolves to form H2CO3, which dissociates in water.)
questions.answer: More CO2 dissolves, forming more H2CO3, which dissociates more to give H+ ions; the equilibrium shifts right, so seawater becomes more acidic (lower pH)
steps: CO2(g) <=> CO2(aq), and CO2(aq) + H2O <=> H2CO3(aq)
H2CO3(aq) <=> H+(aq) + HCO3-(aq)
More atmospheric CO2 dissolves, so the concentration of H2CO3 increases
The dissociation equilibrium shifts to the right to use up H2CO3
More H+ ions are produced, so the seawater becomes more acidic

questions.question: For NO2(g) <=> N2O4(g) at equilibrium in a sealed container, which statement is not true? A the concentrations are constant, B the total number of molecules is constant, C the forward and reverse reactions have both stopped, D the forward and reverse rates are equal.
questions.answer: C (the forward and reverse reactions have both stopped)
steps: At equilibrium the reactions continue at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium)
Concentrations and total molecules stay constant, so A, B and D are true
The reactions have not stopped, so C is the statement that is not true

questions.question: Which statement is not true for a system at dynamic equilibrium? A the position of equilibrium is affected by temperature, pressure and catalysts, B the concentration of reactants is constant, C the forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates, D the equilibrium can be reached from either direction.
questions.answer: A (catalysts do not change the position of equilibrium)
steps: A catalyst changes the rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally
A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the equilibrium yield
Temperature and pressure can change the position of equilibrium, but catalysts cannot
So statement A is not true

questions.question: Describe how London forces arise.
questions.answer: Random movement of electrons creates a temporary dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, giving a weak attraction
steps: Electrons in a molecule move randomly, so at any instant the electron distribution is uneven
This creates a temporary (instantaneous) dipole
The temporary dipole induces an opposite dipole in a neighbouring molecule
The resulting weak attraction between the dipoles is a London force

questions.question: State why the London forces in HI are stronger than those in HCl and HBr.
questions.answer: HI has more electrons (a larger, more polarisable electron cloud), so its London forces are stronger
steps: HI has more electrons than HCl or HBr
More electrons give a larger, more polarisable electron cloud
Larger induced dipoles give stronger London forces

questions.question: The boiling temperature of hydrogen fluoride is +20 C. State what causes this unusually high boiling temperature.
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonding between HF molecules
steps: HF has H bonded to highly electronegative F
This gives strong hydrogen bonds between HF molecules
Much more energy is needed to overcome hydrogen bonds than London forces

questions.question: Explain, using oxidation numbers, why the reaction of chlorine with water (Cl2 + H2O <=> HCl + HClO) is a disproportionation reaction.
questions.answer: Chlorine (oxidation number 0) is both oxidised to +1 in HClO and reduced to -1 in HCl, so it is a disproportionation
steps: Oxidation number of Cl in Cl2 is 0
In HCl, Cl has oxidation number -1, so Cl is reduced
In HClO, Cl has oxidation number +1, so Cl is oxidised
The same element is both oxidised and reduced, so this is a disproportionation

questions.question: State and explain what happens to the position of equilibrium when NaOH(aq) is added to the chlorine and water equilibrium mixture.
questions.answer: The equilibrium shifts to the right, because OH- removes H+ ions (from HCl and HClO), lowering the H+ concentration
steps: NaOH adds OH- ions to the mixture
OH- reacts with H+ ions (from HCl and HClO) to form water
Lowering the H+ concentration removes a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the right
More HCl and HClO form

questions.question: The conversion of ethene to ethanol is 5% at equilibrium but the overall yield is 95%. Suggest what happens to the equilibrium mixture so that the overall yield becomes 95%.

The equilibrium mixture is cooled and the ethanol is separated out
The unreacted ethene and steam are recycled back to the reactor
Repeated passes give an overall yield of 95%

questions.question: Explain why the temperature of 300 C used in the hydration of ethene is a compromise.
questions.answer: Higher temperature increases the rate but decreases the equilibrium yield (exothermic), so 300 C balances rate and yield
steps: The hydration of ethene is exothermic
Higher temperature increases the rate of reaction
But higher temperature shifts equilibrium to the left, lowering the yield of ethanol
Lower temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate, so 300 C is a compromise

questions.question: Explain why a manufacturer might suggest a pressure greater than 7 MPa.
questions.answer: Higher pressure increases the equilibrium yield (2 gas moles to 1), but costs of equipment and energy rise, so 7 MPa is the compromise
steps: Gas moles: C2H4 + H2O = 2 mol; C2H5OH = 1 mol
Higher pressure shifts equilibrium right, increasing the yield of ethanol
Higher pressure also increases the rate of reaction
However, high-pressure equipment and compression are expensive, so 7 MPa is a compromise

questions.question: At pressures greater than 7 MPa, a waxy solid forms which melts over a range of temperatures. Identify this solid.
questions.answer: Poly(ethene) (a polymer formed from ethene)
steps: At high pressure ethene polymerises as a side reaction
The product is a long-chain polymer, poly(ethene)
Polymers melt over a range of temperatures because chain lengths vary

questions.question: Give one other reason for not operating the process at a pressure greater than 7 MPa, not including safety considerations.
questions.answer: Higher pressure needs more energy and more expensive equipment (compression costs), making the process uneconomic; it also increases the waxy polymer by-product that blocks the catalyst
steps: Compressing the gases to higher pressure needs more energy
Equipment that withstands high pressure is more expensive to build and run
The polymer by-product coats the catalyst and reduces its activity

questions.topic: Advantage and Disadvantage of Excess Water
questions.question: Increasing the amount of water in the reaction mixture, without changing the pressure, might be suggested. Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage.
questions.answer: Advantage: more water reduces polymer (waxy solid) formation and shifts equilibrium right; disadvantage: dilutes the ethene, lowering the rate, and more energy is needed to separate and heat the extra water
steps: Advantage: extra water shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of ethanol
Advantage: more water reduces the formation of the waxy polymer by-product
Disadvantage: dilution lowers the concentration of ethene, so the rate of reaction falls
Disadvantage: more energy is needed to heat and then separate the extra water from the product

questions.question: For the methane and steam equilibrium (endothermic forward reaction), what is the effect of lowering the temperature? A rate increases, yield increases; B rate increases, yield decreases; C rate decreases, yield increases; D rate decreases, yield decreases.
questions.answer: D (rate decreases, yield decreases)
steps: Lower temperature gives lower kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have E >= Ea and the rate falls
The forward reaction (methane and steam) is endothermic
Lowering temperature shifts equilibrium to the left, so the yield falls
The answer is D

questions.question: For the methane and steam equilibrium, what is the effect of increasing the pressure? A rate increases, yield increases; B rate increases, yield decreases; C rate decreases, yield increases; D rate decreases, yield decreases.
questions.answer: B (rate increases, yield decreases)

CH4 + H2O (2 mol gas) gives CO + 3H2 (4 mol gas) in the forward reaction
Higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles, which is the left
Yield decreases, so the answer is B

questions.topic: Thermal Stability and Cost of CaCO3
questions.question: Explain, with reference to the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates, why using calcium carbonate rather than magnesium carbonate would increase the cost of the process.
questions.answer: CaCO3 is more thermally stable (Ca2+ is larger with lower charge density), so it needs a higher temperature to decompose, requiring more energy and fuel
steps: Ca2+ is larger than Mg2+ with the same 2+ charge, so it has lower charge density
A lower charge density cation polarises the carbonate ion less
So CaCO3 is more thermally stable and decomposes only at a higher temperature
A higher furnace temperature needs more energy (fuel), which increases the cost

questions.question: Explain why the industrial production of methanol from CO2 + 3H2 <=> CH3OH + H2O (delta H = -49.5 kJ mol-1) uses a pressure of 50 atmospheres and a temperature of 250 C.
questions.answer: 50 atm gives a higher yield (4 gas moles to 2) and faster rate but costs are acceptable; 250 C gives a reasonable rate and catalyst activity, although lower temperature would favour yield (exothermic)
steps: Gas moles: CO2 + 3H2 = 4 mol on the left; CH3OH + H2O = 2 mol on the right
High pressure shifts equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of methanol
The 50 atm pressure balances higher yield against the cost of high-pressure equipment
The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature would favour yield
250 C is a compromise that gives a fast enough rate and an active copper catalyst while keeping yield reasonable
